Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Britain's House of Lords voted Wednesday to suspend two of its members over corruption claims -- the first time a lord has been barred from the chamber since 1642, a spokesman for the chamber said. Britain's House of Lords voted to suspend two of its members. It's first time a lord has been barred since 1642. Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott allegedly agreed to use their influence to get a loophole into a proposed tax law in exchange for cash, but the person offering the bribe turned out to be an undercover reporter. The Sunday Times newspaper ran the sting operation, in which journalists approached members of the House of Lords, claiming to be acting on behalf of a foreign business looking to open a chain of stores in the United Kingdom. "Secret recordings showed Lord Truscott, a former energy minister, discussing a fee of up to $113,000 to work 'behind the scenes' on behalf of the lobbyists, while Lord Taylor offered to conduct a campaign to persuade ministers and officials for a one-year retainer of $189,000," the newspaper said. "Neither peer took any money or offered to [introduce] an amendment themselves." Truscott and Taylor were among four lords investigated by the House of Lords Sub-Committee on Interests. The ethics panel found last week that Truscott "was advertising his power and willingness to influence parliament in order for substantial financial inducement." He called the verdict "outrageous and slanderous," according to the official report by the panel, which rejected his appeal against the decision. Taylor said he knew the journalists were running a sting operation and that he made "increasingly extravagant and outlandish claims in an effort to 'flush out' the truth," according to the official Lords report on the incident. The ethics committee considered his defense "full of internal contractions" and found him in breach of the Lords Code of Conduct. Two other lawmakers, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape, were found not to have breached the code. The suspension of Truscott and Taylor is officially for breaching the Code of Conduct, which states that members are required to "always act on their personal honor." They will not face criminal charges, London's Metropolitan Police said. The suspension will last until the next session of parliament begins in November. Only the Queen can permanently strip a lord of his title. Both Taylor and Truscott are associated with the governing Labor Party. Thomas Taylor joined the House of Lords, the upper house of parliament, in 1978. Peter Truscott got his baronage in 2004. Their historic suspension comes a day after the speaker of the House of Commons, the lower house of parliament, was forced to resign -- the first such resignation in more than 300 years. CNN's Nicola Goulding contributed to this report.

Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott were accused of offering to use their political influence to secure a loophole in proposed tax legislation in return for payment. However, the supposed lobbyist offering the money was actually an undercover journalist.

The Sunday Times organized the operation. Its reporters approached several members of the House of Lords while pretending to represent an overseas company that wanted to establish a chain of stores in the United Kingdom.

The committee’s official report said Truscott described that finding as “outrageous and slanderous.” His appeal was rejected.

According to the Lords’ official account, he said he responded with progressively more exaggerated and implausible statements in an attempt to expose what was happening. The committee found his explanation internally contradictory and ruled that he had violated the Lords Code of Conduct.

The other two peers investigated, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape, were cleared of breaching the code.

Their suspensions will remain in place until Parliament’s next session starts in November. A peer can be permanently deprived of his title only by the Queen.

Both men are affiliated with the governing Labour Party. Thomas Taylor entered the House of Lords, Parliament’s upper chamber, in 1978, while Peter Truscott received his barony in 2004.

The investigation followed a Sunday Times undercover operation in which reporters posed as lobbyists seeking changes to a bill. Secret recordings appeared to show some peers discussing how they could contact ministers, officials, or other parliamentarians and help secure amendments for fees running into tens of thousands of pounds.

The allegations raised serious concerns because members of the House of Lords are prohibited from accepting payment in return for advocating a particular legislative outcome. Although peers may undertake outside employment and provide political advice, they must not use their parliamentary office as part of a paid lobbying arrangement. # UK House of Lords suspends two peers over “cash for influence” allegations

**LONDON, England —** Britain’s House of Lords has suspended two members accused of offering to use their positions to influence legislation in return for payment, in one of the chamber’s most serious disciplinary actions in centuries.

Lord Truscott and Lord Taylor of Blackburn were each suspended for six months after fellow peers approved findings that they had breached the House’s code of conduct.

The allegations emerged from an undercover investigation by *The Sunday Times*, whose reporters posed as representatives of a foreign company seeking changes to proposed legislation. The newspaper alleged that the two Labour peers indicated they could help secure amendments in exchange for fees.

Both men denied wrongdoing.

A Lords committee concluded, however, that Lord Truscott and Lord Taylor had shown a willingness to act as paid advocates — conduct prohibited under parliamentary rules. The committee recommended their suspension, describing their behavior as damaging to public confidence in Parliament.

The vote marked the first time in hundreds of years that members of the House of Lords had been suspended for misconduct.

Lord Truscott, a former energy minister, said he had not offered to table amendments in return for money. Lord Taylor, a veteran Labour politician, also rejected the allegations and criticized the disciplinary process.

The case intensified scrutiny of lobbying and outside financial interests at Westminster. It came amid wider public anger over lawmakers’ expenses and growing demands for tougher parliamentary ethics rules.

The suspensions temporarily bar the two peers from attending House proceedings, voting or claiming parliamentary allowances. They retain their titles and may return once the six-month penalties expire.

## 2009 “cash for influence” suspensions

In May 2009 the House of Lords suspended two Labour peers—**Lord Truscott** and **Lord Taylor of Blackburn**—after a *Sunday Times* undercover investigation into paid lobbying. It was the first use of suspension against peers for centuries, commonly described at the time as the first such action since 1642.

### The sting

Reporters posing as representatives of a business approached several peers about securing changes to legislation. Secret recordings showed:

- **Lord Truscott**, a former energy minister, discussing a consultancy arrangement reportedly worth about **£72,000 a year** and ways of obtaining an amendment, including approaching ministers and other parliamentarians.
- **Lord Taylor** discussing a fee of as much as **£120,000 a year** and claiming he could use his contacts and influence to help achieve the desired change.

Two other peers investigated after the articles, **Lord Moonie** and **Lord Snape**, were not found to have breached the rules.

### Their defenses

Both Truscott and Taylor denied agreeing to sell parliamentary influence.

- **Truscott** argued that he was offering legitimate strategic or consultancy advice based on his experience, not promising personally to table an amendment or misuse his position. He also criticized the undercover operation and said parts of the conversations had been taken out of context.
- **Taylor** said he had been exaggerating his influence and “bigging himself up” to prospective clients. He maintained that no contract was signed, no money changed hands and no parliamentary action was ultimately taken.

### Ethics findings

The **Sub-Committee on Lords’ Interests**, whose conclusions were endorsed by the **Committee for Privileges**, relied heavily on the recordings and transcripts. It rejected the peers’ characterization of the talks as ordinary consultancy.

The committees concluded that each man had demonstrated a willingness, in return for payment, to exercise parliamentary influence. That breached the Lords’ rule against **paid advocacy**—even though no payment was made and no amendment was actually secured. The inquiry did not treat every boast made during the recorded conversations as proven fact, but found the offers themselves sufficiently clear to constitute serious misconduct.

### Penalties

On **21 May 2009**, the House approved the recommended sanctions:

- **Lord Truscott** was suspended for approximately six months.
- **Lord Taylor of Blackburn** was likewise excluded for roughly six months, through the remainder of the 2008–09 parliamentary session.

The sanctions barred them from attending proceedings and using the House’s facilities during the suspension. The episode was constitutionally significant because the Lords had to affirm its authority to suspend members and had not imposed such a punishment in modern parliamentary history.

# House of Lords suspends two peers in historic “cash-for-influence” ruling

**LONDON, May 21, 2009** — Britain’s House of Lords has suspended two Labour peers after concluding that they were prepared to use their positions to influence legislation in return for payment—the chamber’s first such suspensions since 1642.

Lord Truscott, a former energy minister, was barred from the Lords for six months. Lord Taylor of Blackburn, a veteran Labour peer, was suspended for the remainder of the parliamentary session. Both denied wrongdoing, but peers overwhelmingly approved the sanctions recommended by the House’s Committee for Privileges.

The case arose from a *Sunday Times* undercover investigation in which reporters posed as lobbyists seeking changes to the Business Rate Supplements Bill. According to the inquiry, the two peers discussed helping the supposed clients secure amendments or other legislative assistance in exchange for substantial consultancy fees.

Lord Truscott discussed a possible annual payment of about **£72,000**, while Lord Taylor spoke about a retainer of as much as **£120,000 a year**. No money changed hands, and neither peer ultimately introduced the proposed amendments. The Lords’ finding, however, was that their apparent willingness to provide parliamentary influence for payment breached the chamber’s code of conduct.

Members of the Lords may undertake paid work outside Parliament and can advise businesses on policy. They are forbidden, however, from accepting payment to lobby ministers, influence other parliamentarians or shape legislation in a client’s interests. That line—between legitimate consultancy and paid advocacy—was central to the case.

Investigators concluded that Lord Truscott and Lord Taylor had crossed it by indicating that they could use their parliamentary roles, contacts and knowledge of the legislative process to obtain results for paying clients. The committee found the allegations against them substantiated and described their conduct as damaging to public confidence in Parliament.

Two other Labour peers caught up in the newspaper investigation, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape, were not suspended after the committee ruled that the evidence did not establish comparable breaches.

The punishments are historically significant because the Lords had not suspended members for misconduct since **1642**, at the beginning of the English Civil War, when peers associated with the royalist cause were barred from sitting. In modern times, the unelected chamber had generally relied on reprimands, political pressure and voluntary withdrawal rather than formally excluding a peer.

The sanctions do **not** strip either man of his peerage. They temporarily remove the right to sit, vote and claim parliamentary attendance expenses. At the time, life peerages could not ordinarily be revoked, making suspension the strongest practical punishment available short of criminal proceedings or exceptional legislation.

The ruling comes amid a broader crisis over parliamentary ethics, with public anger already mounting over MPs’ expenses. Supporters of the suspensions said the Lords needed to demonstrate that membership did not place peers beyond meaningful discipline.

Both men maintained that they had been discussing legitimate consultancy work rather than selling votes or amendments. The House nevertheless accepted the committee’s judgment that their conversations amounted to an improper offer of parliamentary services for financial reward.

The decision therefore marks both a punishment for the two peers and a constitutional milestone: for the first time in more than three and a half centuries, the House of Lords has used its authority to bar members from the chamber for misconduct.

# Cash for Influence: The Undercover Investigation That Shook the House of Lords

An undercover newspaper investigation into four Labour peers in 2009 exposed weaknesses in the rules governing lobbying and outside interests in the House of Lords. The affair culminated in the suspension of Lord Truscott and Lord Taylor of Blackburn—an exceptional punishment that revived debate over whether Parliament was capable of policing itself.

Reporters from *The Sunday Times*, posing as lobbyists acting for a foreign business, approached four Labour-associated members of the Lords: Lord Moonie, Lord Snape, Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott. They asked whether the peers could help secure changes to proposed legislation, including the Business Rate Supplements Bill, in return for consultancy payments.

Recordings published by the newspaper appeared to show discussions about fees and ways of influencing the legislative process. The investigation alleged that payments worth tens of thousands of pounds were contemplated, with some proposed arrangements reaching six figures.

The central issue was not whether the peers were entitled to hold outside jobs. Members of the House of Lords were permitted to undertake consultancy work, provided that relevant interests were declared. The more serious question was whether they had offered to use their parliamentary position to alter legislation for a client—conduct prohibited by the chamber’s rules.

## Parliamentary inquiry

The allegations were examined by the Lords’ standards machinery and the Committee for Privileges. Its conclusions distinguished sharply between the four men.

Lord Moonie and Lord Snape were not found to have breached the relevant rules. Although their conversations with the undercover reporters attracted criticism, the evidence was judged insufficient to establish that they had agreed to exercise parliamentary influence in return for payment.

The committee reached a different conclusion in the cases of Lord Truscott, a former energy minister, and Lord Taylor. It found that both had shown a willingness to provide parliamentary services for financial reward and had therefore breached the House’s code of conduct.

Both peers disputed the most damaging interpretation of their actions. Nevertheless, the House approved six-month suspensions for each of them in May 2009. The sanctions were historically significant: suspension of members had been so rare that the decision was widely described as the first such punishment imposed on peers for centuries.

## Why the case mattered

The scandal illustrated the risks created by the Lords’ unusual institutional structure. Unlike members of the House of Commons, most peers did not receive a conventional parliamentary salary. Many maintained careers in business, law, public affairs and consultancy. Supporters of this system argued that it brought valuable expertise into Parliament. Critics said it blurred the boundary between legitimate professional experience and paid access to political power.

The undercover operation also demonstrated how difficult that boundary could be to enforce. No amendment needed to be passed—and no payment necessarily completed—for public confidence to be damaged. The suggestion that a legislator might market access, influence or procedural knowledge was itself corrosive.

Labour, then in government, faced particular embarrassment because all four peers were associated with the party. Yet the affair went beyond party politics. It raised a broader constitutional question: whether an unelected chamber, whose members often had extensive commercial interests, possessed sufficiently clear rules and sufficiently independent enforcement.

## A wider crisis of trust

The investigation emerged during a period of declining confidence in Westminster, shortly before the parliamentary expenses scandal transformed public attitudes toward political accountability. Together, such controversies reinforced the impression that Parliament’s internal culture had tolerated practices that ordinary voters regarded as unacceptable.

The suspensions of Lord Truscott and Lord Taylor were therefore important not only as punishment but as precedent. They showed that the Lords was prepared to impose serious sanctions on its own members. At the same time, the need for an undercover newspaper operation to bring the conduct to light exposed the limitations of disclosure-based regulation and self-policing.

The episode remains a notable case study in parliamentary corruption and influence-peddling. It demonstrated that corruption need not take the simple form of cash handed over for a vote. It can arise through consultancy agreements, privileged access and offers to shape legislation behind the scenes. The lasting lesson was that declarations of interest alone are insufficient: Parliament also needs clear boundaries, credible investigations and sanctions strong enough to deter members from treating public office as a commercial asset.
